utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. I think we all together are a bit responsible for the late start. There were some problems of -- about the protective measures that would apply. But, first of all, Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The next witness to be examined is called for cross-examination. His testimony has been admitted under Rule 92 bis. The Chamber has granted a request for protective measures which was formulated as -- that a Chamber should order that the identities -- the identity and the identifying information for that witness would not be disclosed to the public. To translate that in practical measures during cross-examination would mean face distortion, voice distortion, and pseudonym. That is how the Chamber interprets now its own decision. And perhaps when a similar request is made, perhaps it could be formulated a bit more precise, also in case cross-examination -- in case the witness would be called for cross-examination. Mr. Stewart, are you ready to cross-examine Witness 012?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Your Honour. But I also have a -- a specific and un -- unusual request which I've discussed with the Prosecution, and the -- the position is this, Your Honour: Your Honours I think are probably well aware - she's informed you herself from time to time - that Ms. Loukas has an outstanding application for her to be -- to withdraw as co-counsel. And for -- for the record, but without wishing there to be any misunderstanding, I now also have an application for her to be withdrawn, but I must make it clear that's not a hostile application in any form as between Ms. Loukas and myself if that could give rise to misunderstanding. So there are two pending applications. Your Honour, I don't pre-empt at all the Registrar's decision in -- in this area. It's under consideration and we're told that that will be resolved quite soon. But, Your Honour, in anticipation and in preparation for such a step, if it should come about, I have made arrangements, of course, for a prospective replacement co-counsel. Your Honour, he has flown over this morning from England. And when I say "this morning," it's pretty obvious that means pretty early in England. His flight was at 6.00 this morning from Luton airport. He is coming with me to see Mr. Krajisnik late today. But, Your Honour, part of the purpose of his coming over so early this morning - and we consider it to be a valuable purpose - was that he would have an opportunity of observing this trial in action. Your Honour, I understand that the technical reasons related to the particular courtroom that we're in at the moment, the combination of protective measures which has been granted just makes it technically impossible for him to be in the public gallery, although in theory of course it not being actually closed session, he in principle could and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr -- Mr. Stewart, apart from the time the witness -- the prospective replacement left England, I take it that in the last two minutes you were heading for a solution that he could attend this hearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And so that the public understands and the Trial Chamber understands this very unusual request, Your Honour, I was taking a couple of minutes just to give Your Honour the simple background.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, the position is -- his name is - and I have no reason not to give his name - he couldn't be troubled by that - his name is Mr. David Josse, that is J-o-s-s-e. He is personally known to me as a barrister. He is a member of the bar of England and Wales in good standing, something between 15 and 20 years in practice. He is actually in practice in chambers in England. Your Honour, I'm quite sure -- I see no reason why he wouldn't. I'm quite sure that Mr. Josse would of course give the Trial Chamber any appropriate professional undertaking as a barrister, which is something that of course he would then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- keep to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since it's quite unusual to ask people to speak from the public gallery, when the witness is prepared for being brought in, we could just withdraw for one second and that I personally can take the assurances of Mr. Josse to briefly explain his position and then ask the assurances appropriate at this time, if the parties would agree with that. And then before I'll allow him to enter the -- the public gallery, I'll explain to the witness what the situation is. I think that's fair. Because the witness might be --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Absolute, Your Honour. Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- confused by the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course I have to say the Prosecution, I've discussed it with them, very helpfully agreed entirely with the course that I've proposed. They have no objection. The only other thing I should mention, Your Honour, is we can't find Mr. Josse right now because he may not have arrived from the airport. But we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. As soon as -- as soon as he's there, we'll -- yes. And it's good that you warn us, Mr. Stewart, because I do understand that good behaviour of the Chamber might enhance the chances that Mr. Josse will --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I've said nothing to him, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Nothing to him at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll turn in -- is voice distortion in place? Is face distortion in place? They're all in place. The pseudonym to be used is KRAJ 012, I take it, Mr. Margetts?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, whilst the witness is coming in, this is obviously 92 bis with cross-examination. We would like to introduce two exhibits, one being the annexure to the statement that has been introduced into evidence and another being a press article that the witness brought and provided to us today and we have provided an copy of that article to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is a 92 bis witness. Usually a summary is read into the -- into the transcript, but of course identifying elements should not be in there. I don't know whether there -- has any summary been prepared or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, a summary has been prepared.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And I take it that particular caution has been given to the -- that the potential identifying elements are -- are not present in --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then you'll perhaps explain to the witness the -- the procedure of 92 bis in reading the summary so that he can be present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Witness 012. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 012, because that's how we will address you, the Chamber has granted protective measures, which means that no one outside this courtroom can see your face, no one outside this courtroom can hear your own voice. Your voice will be distorted. And we'll not use your name but we'll address you by "Witness 012." Witness 012, before you give evidence in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by the usher. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness 012. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 012, that no one can see your face, also the public gallery in this courtroom is closed. There is a chance, however, that during this morning's session someone would arrive who is a prospective replacement for Defence counsel; that is, he's a professional lawyer. That might be present. He is expected to be on the Defence team, so he's not just someone of the public but has a very specific reason why he would like to attend. May I take it that you would not oppose if that person but that person alone would be in the public gallery if he arrives this morning?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Even now we switch to channel 4, I did not receive any --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please repeat what you just said, because the interpreters ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my conversations with the Prosecutor so far, I was not informed about that. And I do not want that person to be present, and I can explain why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please tell us why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I explain to you. This person is someone who is expected to join the Defence team. Defence lawyers --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Sorry, just -- the previous answer from the witness may tend to identify him. If we could have that redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it will be redacted. This is a professional lawyer who comes from England, just as Mr. Stewart, Defence counsel, is a professional lawyer who comes from England. So he's not someone that could possibly be expected to interfere. He is someone who will expectedly join the Defence team. And Defence counsel of course are here, see your face, hear your voice. So therefore I again would like to ask you. It would be different if it was someone unknown. It is a professional lawyer from a non-Balkan country with good standing for over, many, many years. And I will instruct that person, if he arrives, personally that whatever he sees - because that's the only difference, that he sees your face - that he should not talk about it to anyone. So I do not see at this moment how that would add in whatever way to the security -- that to keep him out would add in whatever way to the security of your family. And you may accept from me that this Chamber is sharp on protection of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's very hard for me to change my opinion within the scope of two or five minutes. I adhere to what I have just said. If I acted differently, I would undermine myself. I fully appreciate what you have just said. However, this -- if this had been said to me in time, I would have considered that opportunity. And as things stand now, I don't see why I should accept this situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, before we give any final decision on the issue, I suggest the following: That we start now. As soon as the Chamber is informed that Mr. Josse has arrived - and if that would be before the first break - but otherwise that we would allow the Prosecution to speak with the witness during the first break on the subject only of this matter. They can be assisted by interpreters so that, Mr. Margetts, you're in a better position perhaps to explain the situation and that we do not take any decision as it is now. So public gallery at this moment is empty. And whenever Mr. Josse would arrive, if that would be before -- before the first break, we'll wait until the first break. During the first break, Mr. Margetts, you are - with your consent, Mr. Stewart - allowed to discuss this matter, this matter only, with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I couldn't possibly object to that course because the Prosecution have been distinctly helpful over this matter. If we should get to that point, Your Honour, it might be that I would appreciate being able to say something very briefly which would be better said probably in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, shall we cross that bridge -- I should just say that although perhaps Mr. Josse is not yet in the building, I spoke to him early this morning as he was about to get on the plane. So the likelihood that he's seriously delayed is not very high because he was just boarding the plane when I spoke to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber has taken no decision, so at this moment you can be assured there's no one who can see your face, not even on an exceptional basis. Mr. Margetts, you explained to the witness the 92 bis procedure and that you'll read out a summary?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Just a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, of course you'd first like to start with the identity of the witness, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just to comment on the matter we've just discussed. I did explain to the witness that in this courtroom should these protective measures be in place then the public gallery would be empty. So the course that Your Honour has indicated, I think, is the appropriate one, that I explain why there may be an exception to that. Your Honour, if we could present the first exhibit, the pseudonym sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The pseudonym sheet will be Prosecution Exhibit P728, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Witness 12, can you read the document before you. Does your name and your date of birth appear on that document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: I've finished with that exhibit. If we could move to the next exhibit, which is the attachment to the ICTY statement of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that the Chamber will receive everything as a package on a CD, so the statement would then get one number and whatever is attached to it gets a related number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The situation was that this was not -- was not specifically requested that this be part of the 92 bis package, and that's the reason that I'm presenting it in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: -- in this manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The attachment to the ICTY witness statement will be Prosecution Exhibit number P729.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just have a couple of questions in relation to this exhibit. And if we could go into private session so I could ask those questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness 012, the Chamber has observed that where the Chamber thought that it would not make that much of a difference, that it's disturbed you and that it confused you and that you opposed strongly against the presence of even one person in the public gallery. For that reason, although we gave an opportunity to the Prosecution to discuss the matter with you, the Chamber finally decides whether you would have given your consent or whether you would not have given your consent, that the presence of that person is not of such importance as that would justify to take any risk that you would feel put under pressure to agree with something you rather would not agree to. Therefore, whatever your position would have been, the Chamber meanwhile has decided, taking into consideration your earlier response, not to make any exception to what has been told to you. Also, in order to avoid that you get the feeling that something different is told to you prior to the court and then suddenly the situation in court would change unexpectedly for you. So, therefore, no exceptions are allowed. And, Mr. Margetts, you may proceed. But then we -- we'll turn into private session, since we are dealing with a document that might contain identifying detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: The following is the 92 bis summary of the statements that have been admitted into evidence for Witness KRAJ 012. The witness was a high-ranking member of a municipality in the Romanija region. In May 1991, the SDS municipality leaders established a "Community of Municipalities," incorporating immediately surrounding municipalities. By autumn of 1991, the Serbian Autonomous Region of Romanija had been established. From early 1992, Serbian paramilitaries trained volunteers in the municipality and by the end of February 1992, two brigades of paramilitaries had been organised. At the end of February 1992, weapons were distributed to hundreds of Serbs by the Serbian commander of the Territorial Defence. In March 1992, all of the non-Serb officers were dismissed from the police and the Serb police of SAO Romanija was formed. Zoran Cvijetic was appointed Minister of Internal Affairs of SAO Romanija. In March 1992, all non-Serbs were dismissed from public positions. At a meeting between Serb and Muslim representatives, the Serbs stated that those who were not prepared to obey the Serb authority would be killed or expelled. The president of the Municipality and president of the Serb Crisis Staff stated that this would be the last meeting with the Muslims, since the Muslims "won't exist any longer." Following this meeting, many crimes took place in the municipality and the Serbs prepared a list of wanted persons, including the witness, who they said were enemies of the Serbian State. The witness left the municipality and his family also left the municipality. That concludes the 92 bis summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Witness 012, the main reason why you're in The Hague is since the Defence would like to cross-examine you on the written statement the Chamber has received and has carefully read. And now, Mr. Stewart, counsel for the Defence, will have an opportunity to cross-examine you on this evidence. Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes, we are at the time of a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think it's time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But Mr. Stewart will start only after the break. We'll have a break for half an hour, until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I -- may I begin making a commission while the witness is coming in? Oh, he's coming in anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, he's coming in.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's just this, Your Honour, in relation to that chronology. My submission is this: That it really isn't satisfactory or appropriate even given the reasonable latitude in relation to hearsay evidence that a chronology of events in relation to this municipality should be put in as if it were part of the witness's evidence for a period when he expressly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- acknowledges that he wasn't there. And I'm not going to suggest an issue about the earlier part of the chronology which largely fits in with and supplements in relatively minor ways what's in the statement. But I would suggest, Your Honour, that from -- on that chronology between April 1992 - because the witness says he left in early 1992 - after that, that the rest of that chronology should not be included as the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know whether it's good to fully discuss it in the presence of the witness. Mr. Stewart, I take it that you'll need until the next break approximately for cross-examination at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's -- that's about a good rough estimate, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's then -- let's just then prior to the next break deal with this --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and one or two other matters, because I can imagine that you'd like to know whether that portion of the chronology is admitted into evidence before concluding your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honour, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then please proceed at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, just one matter. And that is Madam Registrar reminded me that we don't have numbers for the statements that have been admitted into evidence. And that may assist the Defence in -- and the Court in the course of the cross-examination, being able to identify those documents by number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The witness statement dated 02 February 1999 will be Prosecution Exhibit P731, under seal. And the addendum to the statement dated 01 May 2003 will be Prosecution Exhibit P731.A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Stewart, you may proceed. And would you please -- may I remind you to switch off the microphone once the witness is answering the question, not before you put the question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, well, I won't do the latter, Your Honour. Sometimes I might. Your Honour, may I just seek a bit of brief guidance. The -- clearly the witness's identity is -- is the issue here. So we're -- we're not in full private session, so my approach must be to try to just avoid anything which points riskily to the witness's identity. Is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's correct. Or ask -- or ask for private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, Your Honour, as an alternative.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness - I have to address you like that without any discourtesy for exactly the reasons of protecting your identity. Witness, you give quite a lot of evidence in the statements about the activities in your municipality and particularly of Serb forces in the most general sense of that meaning. Can you confirm that in the autumn of 1991 there was also a formation of units of a Muslim paramilitary organisation generally known as the Green Berets in Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: This is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So if I suggest that if you think about it, there was such -- there were such units formed headed by a Mr. Mevludin Smajic, then an employee of the MUP, that's simply untrue, is it? Or do you have no recollection? Which is it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: This person worked in Sarajevo. It was not in our territory. And what you said is absolutely not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You're telling the Trial Chamber, are you that, you positively know it to be untrue; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: Absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And so if, for example, Mr. Smajic subsequently admitted later in 1992 that he had brought explosives to Sokolac, distributed them among Muslims, and instructed them how to make bombs, do you know about that or do you say also that that is untrue?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: I know Mr. Smajic personally, and this person likes to brag a lot. He is an unreliable person. And what you are saying has nothing whatsoever to do with the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So Mr. Smajic is such a bragger, is he, that if he told the press and through the press the public that he had brought explosives to Sokolac and distributed them and given instructions how to make bombs, this was false bragging, was it, by Mr. Smajic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it was false bragging. Just like you have put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And if it is suggested that in around December 1991 Mr. Smajic was making lists of prospective Muslim fighters, distributing arms, and reconnoitering the territory of the Romanija region, do you say that you don't know anything about that or that it is positively untrue?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that. But I would like to add to that that it is absolutely untrue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can we get that clear. You don't know anything about it but nevertheless you are willing to assert before this Trial Chamber that it is absolutely untrue? Have I understood your answer correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just -- let me just try to -- just for clarification, Witness, is there a possibility that you do not know about it but that it may have happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This did not happen. Absolutely not. (redacted) Mevludin Smajic, who is a very unstable person. (redacted). And the only thing I know and that I heard and I read in news reports is that Mr. Momcilo Radic [as interpreted] and this person were involved in crimes, in the thefts of cars. And this is what I know about him. I am sure that he was not involved in anything that was mentioned by the Defence. He did not do any such thing. He was not concerned with that at all. He is just a -- a bragger, nothing else. He just brags. That's who he is, a bragger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we have a clarification in respect of the name that appears at page 28, line 23. It was Mr. Momcilo, and I didn't quite catch the surname.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please repeat the name you mentioned, the first name being Mr. Momcilo -- you said, "I heard and I read in news reports" -- no, I'll read the whole line to you: "And the only thing I know and that I heard and I read in news reports is that Mr. Momcilo" and this person "were involved in crimes, in the theft of cars." What is the family name of this person Mr. Momcilo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, two corrections. Not in crimes but in criminal acts. His name was Momcilo Mandic. I don't know whether he was his boss.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Somebody's microphone is on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The press brought reports on these two persons who were involved in criminal acts. They were involved in crime, thefts, forging documents, and other such things. And this is what I heard. And as a person I don't want to waste time in thinking about the two gentlemen that I've mentioned because they are just lowlifes. They are just petty criminals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say I don't want to develop the point in the presence of the witness, but I'd just like to say for the record, Your Honour, that I'd submit that line 17 of the last page was the -- with respect, the wrong time and the wrong place for the Trial Chamber to intervene in counsel's cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, in January -- similarly, in January 1992 was there in Sokolac a Muslim paramilitary unit operational called - and the English version would be - the People's Patriotic League or some such very similar title?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: I'm absolutely unaware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: At such a -- to try and jog your memory -- such a league with a membership of 866 men? That doesn't trigger your memory in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: 866 able-bodied men in the territory of Sokolac municipality do not exist. The mere fact tells you that it is a fabrication. There are -- there are no 866 Muslim able-bodied men in Sokolac.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And no such organisation existed, you say, at January 1992 in Sokolac, whether with that number or with a smaller number of men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: I am absolutely unaware of -- of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: By the end of January 1992, Witness, were there any fighting groups of Muslims in Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: When you say "Muslim fighting units," I can say that they did not exist nor could they have existed, for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, let's be careful about definitions, then. The units I'm asking you about now in this next question, I include any units formed with a view to potential fighting as well as perhaps any actual fighting that they were conducting. And such units, were there -- had there been any that had come into existence during 1991 and 1992 in Sokolac by the end of January 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: No. There was no need for any such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Because there was simply not enough threat from anywhere to create such a need?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: There were even too many threats. However, there was no way to organise any units. It was impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Had there been any discussion in the Muslim community about any possibility or -- of forming any such units or groups?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I also ask you to -- to directly answer the question. The question put to you was whether there had been any discussion in the Muslim community about any possibility of forming any such units or groups. That was the question. Could you please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am unaware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, when do you say -- well, were there at any point in 1992 that Muslim fighting or prospective fighting groups formed in Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were not. And since we are talking about only four and a half thousand people, I'm sure that I would be aware of any such things, because most of the people are relatives, friends, acquaintances. And despite my obligations and my workload, I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the mics please be switched off at all times while the witness is speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mine was, Your Honour, at this time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now it's better. The usher's mic is switched on. The mic near the door, the entrance door.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as I now can see, there's no microphone open any more. If the problem continues, I'd like to be informed. I'll switch off mine now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So throughout 1991 and 1992, did the Muslim community, then, in the municipality of Sokolac continue in a totally defenceless state without any fighting facilities or abilities at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: At that time we could see that there was a war going on in Croatia and that its focus would be moved because a lot of weapons from Slovenia and Croatia was being transferred to Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, as the least numerous people in the former Yugoslavia, Muslims were in favour of Yugoslavia. They trusted the Yugoslav People's Army, which did what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, excuse me. If -- if I wish to put questions to you about the background and the position of the various communities in relation to Yugoslavia and so on, I will put those questions. May I remind you of what my question was: It was whether throughout 1991 and 1992 the Muslim community in the municipality of Sokolac continued in a totally defenceless state without any fighting facilities or abilities at all. That is the question.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: Due to their naivete that I have just explained, the community of 4.500 people, consisting of men, women, and men -- adults and children, people who worked and who were in favour of peace and dignity, they did not believe that -- that what would happen would happen to them and that's why they did not organise themselves, because they did not see the clear threat. They failed to see the clear threat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you've now answered the question which you formulated yourself as why they did not organise themselves. The question was whether they had any facilities created. So first before we go to the why, we first have to establish what actually happened. So Mr. Stewart asked you whether there was no facility of defence whatsoever. It could be anything. Whether that would be from hunting rifles and to tanks or whatever, whether there was nothing at all. And I can inform you that this Chamber has heard some evidence that in many places some type of action by standing guard or buying weapons somewhere or seeing whether still some legitimate weapons were available to defend if it would be necessary or -- but whatever. So we heard that that had happened. At least, we heard evidence that this happened in some municipalities. And therefore, again the question, not the why, but was there nothing of that kind happening in Sokolac? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if people stand guard in front of their house preventing crime -- criminals from entering the house and killing their children, it's not any form of resistance. So I would adhere to my statement when I say that I was not aware of any such thing. No classical units were known. And there were a thousand households. And for me to go from one house to another to see whether anybody was standing guard to protect their unborn -- newborn babies, it was irrelevant for me. I'm not a sociologist. I didn't do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. That's because you're interpreting the questions rather than answering them. Mr. Stewart asked whether there were in totally defenceless state. If you stand guard before your house, even if it was with a hunting rifle or whatever, then that is a state of defence. I'm not saying that there's anything wrong with that. But we are just trying to find the facts. And if someone organises to stand guard, whether it is to protect your families or not, for whatever purpose. We first have to find out what the facts were. And may I just add to that that these questions are not asked to you as to blame someone for whatever happened but just first to find out what actually happened. Standing guard before your house, if it is with -- with or without weapons or is a kind of a form of defence - and it may be totally justified - but we'd like to know what happened, and that's what Mr. Stewart is trying to find out. So could you please tell us, then, if anyone in the Muslim community thought that there was reason not just to expose them to whatever threat there was there, what did they do - perhaps totally justified - but what did they do to avoid that they were in a totally defenceless state?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, your question is very long and requires some observations. Territory -- the territory of Sokolac municipality covers 724.000 square metres. It's a wooded area. It's an enormous area. And four and a half thousand Bosniaks were scattered in 30 to 40 villages. In peacetime, had I had all possible means of transport and communication, I could not have known what was going on 70 kilometres away at the other end of the municipality. For this reason, I really know nothing about any such units. All I can say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, no one asks from you to know what happens at a distance of 40 or 50 kilometres. What the Chamber and what Mr. Stewart would like to know is whether you are aware of anything of the kind I just described, whether you have seen anything of it, whether it's happened in your neighbourhood. Yes or no? And even whatever type of effort even to defend or to prepare for unpleasant situations took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I, with respect, observe that when Your Honour says to the witness: "No one asks you to know what happens at a distance of 40 or 50 kilometres," in an unqualified form that does not necessarily represent the Defence's position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand that. It was more or less a response to what the witness said when he seemed not to -- when he felt that he might be unable to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, we understand that, Your Honour. But just for clarification --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Because, Witness, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we first ask the witness to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Which -- probably, Your Honour, as a precaution -- I'd be entirely happy for Your Honours to do that. Just remind him once again of what it is, the question namely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question is, Witness -- the question is whether you have any knowledge of any type of defence that was organised from the simplest, as I depicted it to you as a couple of neighbours standing guard or whatever, up till whatever other level, or is it that nothing of this kind happened?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, at that time I was an extremely busy man. I was very busy in my job and constantly on the move. Had I observed anything of the kind, I would tell you now. All I can say is based on my experience is that certain individuals tried to protect my families. I did this, and I assume that others did the same, or something similar. However, I am not aware that there was any kind of organisation in place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, can I just be clear. You said you were very busy in your job and constantly on the move. When you say "on the move," do you mean just that you were constantly active or on the go or do you mean that you travelled around in any way in the course of your work? And don't be too specific, please, Witness, in the answer, bearing in mind the identity question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I said I was active, I meant I was moving between my house and my office. In the office, I had three telephones. I had discussions about my job. I had obligations toward my family. That's what I meant when I said I was active. I went to Sarajevo and other places. I was a young man then, full of life and strength, and I wanted to make a good living, and this when you're young can make you get carried away. That's what I meant when I said I was active.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, please don't get carried away with your answers today too much, Witness. I'd like you to focus very much on -- on the questions that I put to you. Did you -- did you move around the municipality of Sokolac in connection with your work?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: (redacted), to Sarajevo in the direction of Olovo. So I moved along the main roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But otherwise not around the municipality of Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did go out, out -- in view of my job I had to leave the municipality and go to other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, I -- I really have asked you here a very simple question about three or four times in a slightly different form, and, with respect, you do keep answering a slightly different question. As His Honour suggested a few minutes ago, you reformulate the question to some other question. It is very simple what I'm asking you. In connection with your work, did you move around and within the municipality of Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: I moved on the territory of Sokolac municipality as well as outside the municipality in other towns because of my job. The work I was doing, my work required it. I won't go into what I was doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's -- Witness -- Witness, in your statement, without going into the details of it -- but in your statement, from the point where you left Sokolac - and you identified that point in 1992 - you then go on to give quite a lot of evidence about what happened in that place where you were no longer present. How far away -- when you left the area, you say - and you give the date, in the first half of 1992 - how far away were you from Sokolac, from the -- the main town in Sokolac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: What period of time are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, perhaps can I -- a lot must have been happening here, Your Honour. Unless Mr. Margetts suggests that there's a difficulty or risk in actually reminding the witness of exactly when he says he left the area, I -- I could do that. It wouldn't seem to me to present a great problem. But I was just being ultra-cautious.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: The month in which he left the area, I think, is okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. That's helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, you say you left Sokolac in April -- or you left the area in April 1992. That's what you -- you said in your evidence by way of your statement. I'm not asking you precisely where you went. How far away did you go, then, from the main town in Sokolac when you left the area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: Thank you. I said that the information presented about the events that occurred from April 1992 until the end of 1995 were collected in Olovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So how far away were you then? When you left the area, how far away was it that you went?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: It was some 20 kilometres away, maybe a little less than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So let's try and be -- be very clear about what your evidence comes to so there's no misunderstanding. Apart from perhaps individual defence of own households and own family, first of all, you are unaware of any formation of any sort of fighting or prospective fighting Muslim group, whether classical or not, in 1991 and 1992 in the municipality of Sokolac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: Absolutely not. I mean, I was absolutely not aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, so that's absolutely correct, you say. And not only are you unaware of such matters, but is it correct that you feel able to assert to this Trial Chamber that that did not happen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: I am not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Does that mean that you acknowledge that this could have happened without your being aware of it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been repeating this question now. This is the fourth or fifth time, I think. And I said that the Bosniak, Muslim community on Sokolac -- on the territory of Sokolac municipality numbered 4.470 until the genocide which was perpetrated. It was 4.472 people. And although, as I explained a little while ago, these people were scattered all over the territory of Sokolac municipality. They knew one another. And I would have had to know -- even were I deaf or blind I would have had to know about it; I would have had to see or hear about it. I am not aware of any such thing happening except what I said about myself, individuals standing guard in front of their own house as individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I do see the answer buried in -- in there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You -- perhaps you'll move to your next subject, because this matter -- this specific matter has been dealt with sufficiently.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You say, Witness, in your statement -- or you talk about the establishment of a Community of Municipalities in May 1991 which only Sokolac, Han Pijesak, and Pale joined in the end with Rogatica and Olovo not agreeing to join. And you described that as having been established by SDS municipality leaders. What do you know about the activities of that Community of Municipalities from May 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: As I have already said, the Community of Municipalities was established in early May, while the euphoria lasted following the establishment of the Serbian Radical Party in a cave on Mount Romanija. This was presided over by Dr. Vojislav Seselj. In this euphoria, this enthusiasm prompted by the myth of some sort of Greater Serbia and probably the project of the SDS leaders concerning all parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina which had a relative Serb majority, Autonomous Provinces were established, Communities of Municipalities which later became Serbian Autonomous Provinces. They had their ministries. They had a Minister of Police; for example, Zoran Cvijetic was the Minister of Police of the Romanija SAO. Slobodan Batinic was the commander of the Territorial Defence. Then there was a minister of information, and that was Nedeljko Zugic, whom I have known since we were schoolchildren because we lived in the students' residence. And there was not much effort to conceal this. It was not only I who knew about it but anyone living in Sokolac municipality who knew anything about things knew about this. The self-declared Serbian Autonomous Province organised line-ups of policemen in March on the stadium in Sokolac municipality - I'm referring to the soccer pitch - where all the citizens could see what was happening. And I saw it as well. And this was attended by several dignitaries of the Republican Ministry of the Interior who were of Serb ethnicity, also the Chief of Police from Pale and --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, may I perhaps, with His Honour's permission, just invite you to stop there in relation to that answer. The -- I'll move to a different topic. You say that in May 1991 the firms and factories in the municipality - and that's Sokolac - stopped paying taxes for pensions and medical treatment to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and started sending the payments to Serbia. Now, first, being careful not to give away any identifying information, did that change happen where you worked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: Where the chief accountants were Muslims, it didn't happen. They respected the laws of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. But in those companies where Serbs were in the majority, the chief accountants, the chief executive, the managers, they directed the payments towards Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what is the source of your knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: In the town of Sokolac municipality, there were 208 Bosniaks and the managers, managing directors, and other executives who were Serbs felt so comfortable that they made no effort to conceal this. I heard from them on more than one occasion that they were doing this. I also learned about it later on, after the war, when our people went to Sarajevo to get the documents relating to their pensions, when they were collecting documents either to get a new job or to retire. And all the people I talked to discovered that their pension insurance payments had not been paid in Sarajevo in that period, say 1990-1991-1992. And in this way the misfortune of these people is continuing, even 13 years later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You also say in your statement that in that period and your reference point is there is May 1991, that "every 15 to 20 days meetings of the leaders of municipalities inhabited by Serbs were held in Belgrade." My first question, Witness, is: What is the source of your information in relation to that matter?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: I learned about it from people who went there, municipal officers, and when talking to businessmen and other people, they would say, We had a meeting about the electrical power plants in the then-Titovo Uzice, or they would say, We had a meeting in Belgrade about this or about that. So it was not difficult to reach this conclusion. Not only is it known to me; it's well known to anyone engaged in any kind of business activity at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then you say - this is paragraph 12, by the way - but you say that "all business and payments were turned towards Belgrade." Are you -- is that just a summary of what you -- you've already described about taxes, pensions, and these reports from businesspeople of meetings in Belgrade, or is there something more that you've got in mind there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: There were many events which I summarised here. Let me just say that replacing the Yugoslav dinar with some kind of Serb dinar is another illustration of this. The banks injected para-currency, illegal currency, and this only goes to show how serious this plan was and how complete, encompassing the economy, culture. For example, if some kind of cultural event was organised, there were no contacts with Sarajevo or neighbouring municipalities but only with Belgrade. Shops from Belgrade opened their shops here. The newspapers no longer came from Sarajevo. The TV was forcibly oriented toward Belgrade. And this is generally well known. There was a system put in place which created an economic, political, media, information infrastructure, military, police, and other prerequisites for a state which might be called a Greater Serbia. I was a witness of all these events, and I am an intelligent man. I was able to realise what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, in that same paragraph of your statement, after your reference to "all businesses and payments being turned towards Belgrade," you said: "They said" - which seems to refer to leaders of municipalities in your statement but - "They said that they had become a part of an economic community with its centre in Titovo Uzice in Serbia." Witness, we can agree about this, can't we: Yugoslavia - and I'm talking about Yugoslavia as it was then, before these wars - Yugoslavia had been extremely recently a communist state, hadn't it? We can agree about that, can't we?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: Yes, it was a communist state. However, it was organised on a federal principle. There is a difference there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness. Witness, yes, all right. I'm going to discourage you from the howevers. I just wanted to get some simple agreement on that. And the first free elections had been held in November 1990, hadn't they? We can agree about that as well, can't we?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, I don't want to ask you broad sociological and economic questions. But as an intelligent man, you would agree with this, would you: It would have been absolutely remarkable if there hadn't been widespread, significant changes in the structure and nature of economic activity in these countries throughout 1991, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know Mr. Stewart expressed his wish not to ask wide questions of that nature which call for speculation, but in -- in our submission, that -- this witness answering that question would not be helpful to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's an entirely appropriate question because this witness, when he talks in his statement about businesses and payments being turned towards Belgrade in general terms, gives the evidence that he's given, talks about these -- it's hearsay evidence but talks about reports to him of people becoming part of an economic community, it is an entirely legitimate point to pursue in this limited way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness may answer the question. At the same time, we should not stay too long with this subject, which is only marginal of relevance for what the case is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I had no intention of staying on this subject. If the witness answers my question here, we can probably immediately move to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart asked you whether it was -- would have been surprising, if not changes -- significant changes in the structure and the nature of economic activities in these countries would have taken place. That was the question of Mr. Stewart. Could you answer that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a very difficult and very complex question and only an expert would be able to answer that. However, as a person who resided in the area and who was engaged in business, who was part of the business community and who was aware of some things that were happening, I can say only this: The former Yugoslavia was organised on a federal principle. There were some economic dealings on republican principles. So if we're talking about the municipality of Sokolac, it was not a company from Serbia that organised and established a company in Sokolac. It was a Sarajevo company, a Sarajevo corporation that established a company in Sokolac. Planika, a shoe factory from Belgrade, did not establish a company in Knezina. It was the KTK from Visoko, from Bosnia-Herzegovina who established a shoe factory. The first consequence was that companies were alienated from their corporations and their executives started leaning on Serbia. That's one form of theft that is still going on. And I also mentioned culture. But let's mention the medical field. In Sarajevo, there is a clinical hospital, Kosevo, which is renowned all over Europe. And patients from Sokolac were no longer sent to Sarajevo, which is only 40 kilometres away; they would be sent to Belgrade with no reason whatsoever. A whole study could be drafted with -- about that. And I believe that it will be drafted eventually about the idea of alienating everything that belonged -- used to belong to Bosnia and Herzegovina. And for that reason I am saying all this, because I had noticed that all the payments were directed towards Serbia. If we are -- we're talking about the system of payment, banks were not involved in payments. There was a so-called Transaction Payments Institute. Maybe the European, western economists are not aware of that. So this was this service, the SDK or the Payments Transactions Institute, that was in Sarajevo. And any payment that went via Belgrade was against the law at the time. In all the spheres of life, people broke laws. They robbed their companies. For example, electricity that was produced in Bosnia and Herzegovina all of a sudden started being channelled towards Serbia. This is a very difficult and complex question. However, the few examples that I have given you may have helped you to understand things. And if you want me to provide you with some more detail, I am -- I will only be glad to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, you've -- you've said that in all the spheres of life people broke laws. Do you have any knowledge of the -- the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina ceasing to pay its proper dues to the central government in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: What happened to Bosnia and Herzegovina is a miracle, but it was the last republic that continued paying a 3 per cent contribution for the JNA. There was a law in the former Yugoslavia pursuant to which 3 per cent of the total income was allocated for the JNA, and it was only Bosnia and Herzegovina that paid that contribution. Another thing of some significance is the following: There was a law on assistance to Montenegro after the earthquake that had happened in that country, and the only state --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, could you please answer the question. The question was not whether Bosnia and Herzegovina paid the 3 per cent contribution but the question was whether there was any payment that was not done by Bosnia and Herzegovina, payments due to the central government in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, maybe I don't have enough information. This stopped when the infrastructure system imploded and payments no longer could be made. But people in Bosnia and Herzegovina had so much consideration and they were so honest that even when the shelling started, they still had payment slips for payments to be made to various accounts in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, what you're telling us, that there were good reasons to stop paying, the question just was whether there were any payments not made. Could you tell us when it stopped and what payments were stopped.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in my previous statement I said --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that I am not an expert, and it is impossible for me to establish what happened in Sarajevo and when the payments had stopped. However, knowing the people in the place where I resided -- or, for example, in Olovo and so on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you. If I asked you when it stopped: If you do know, tell me; if you don't know, tell me that you don't know. But I was under the impression that you might know, since you gave a rather long answer on payments that were made. So that made me expect that you might also know when it stopped. Do you know it or do you not know it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have to stop you again. The question was about payments made by Bosnia and Herzegovina as one of the republics to the central government in Belgrade. I'm not talking about anything else. Are you aware of any payments due by the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina to the central government that they stopped?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The system was such -- the system of payment was such that all the dues and all the funds - the pension fund, the health insurance fund, all the other contributions, the 3 per cent for the JNA, I don't know how much was paid in respect of Montenegro, 3 or 5 per mil [as interpreted] for the assistance to Montenegro - all those companies that recognised the statehood of Bosnia and Herzegovina continued paying until the 30th March 1992. The dues that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, my question is not about companies paying a state of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I'm talking about payments due by Bosnia and Herzegovina to the central government. Are you aware of those payments being stopped at any specific moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot answer ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I cannot give you a precise answer to that question because at the given moment I was not affiliated with the institutions in Sarajevo that were in charge of that, so there no way for me to know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say you have no precise answer. Do you have an approximate answer? Have you any knowledge on that it stopped in a certain period of time or -- even if you do not know exactly the dates?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Based on the information that I had from talking to people, I can tell you something. I don't know about the last date; however, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was the last to stop paying, of all the republics, Slovenia, Montenegro, and others. Bosnia and Herzegovina was the last that stopped paying its dues to the federal budget, and I don't know when that -- that was. It was the last to stop its payments even towards the JNA of all the republics of the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So, Witness, if I put to you in case it might jog your memory that it was December 1991 following a resolution in the Assembly of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina that that republic ceased paying its proper dues to the central government, you're saying you -- you know -- you know nothing about that; you can't help the Trial Chamber any further on that point? Is that where we are?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: I really can't say anything about that. It would be pure speculation on my part, and that is something I don't want to get involved in.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Let's move on, then, Witness. You say in the next paragraph of your statement - that's paragraph 13 - you referred to the start of the war in Croatia, mobilisation starting in Sokolac and so on. "Bosniaks who were part of the reserve units protested and many of them left their units." When you say "many of them left their units," you mean, do you, that many of them deserted in breach of the law?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: I can say that there was a -- a certain form of forcible mobilisation of everybody and primarily Bosniaks and Croats. These people were sent to the theatres of war in Croatia to fight against the legal bodies of the Republic of Croatia. And if there had been a breach of law, the law was broken by those who sent those units to shell the villages and towns there and to kill people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, let's get it very simple. You talk about forcible mobilisation. Mobilisation, not surprisingly, was compulsory in accordance with the law of Yugoslavia, wasn't it? That's got to be a yes or no -- that must be a yes or no if the first place, Witness, and then you would have ample opportunity to explain in accordance with answering the question properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, from the witness's first answer, we're clearly moving into an area that could be of legal expertise. It did you want seem to me black and white from his previous answer and may not be an appropriate area for this witness to comment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's too limited. Of course, if we're going into further depth, then of course it's -- it certainly would become a legal -- it's anyhow a question to what extent it assists the the Chamber. But the witness may answer this question. The question is, Witness, whether strictly speaking those who left the units were not allowed to do so under the law. And I'm not asking about any good reasons or bad reasons to break that law, but is it true that those who left the units did so by breaking the law? That's the question put to you by Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I know is the following: The mobilised people who were able-bodied men and who were obliged to respond to the mobilisation calls in order to respect the law. The mobilisation place was in Han Pijesak and from there the units were transferred to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And from Banja Luka they were sent to the theatres of war in Croatia. However, in Banja Luka, with Bosniak and Croatian majority, the officers could not move those units. They could not force them to kill people there, and then those units would be returned to Han Pijesak and disbanded. And this is what I had in mind when I was answering the question. The units that could not be used and could not be moved by their officers in order to fight in the Republic of Croatia in the various theatres of war, they would be returned to Han Pijesak and disbanded. And when these units were disbanded in Han Pijesak, all the Muslims were taken their arms away from them, whereas the Serbs were given those weapons either to take home or use in any way they saw fit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I hope Your Honour will see that the -- in this limited area in relation to the basically legalities, this is material to -- what the witness covers in his own statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In paragraph 13 of your own statement, you refer to two different situations, Witness. One is where you say "Bosniaks who were part of reserve units protested and many of them left their units." That's one situation. The second situation is you say: "Some units composed mostly of Bosniaks who were sent to Banja Luka were dismissed and sent back." So that's the second situation. Now, I just want to be -- just see if we can get agreement. The first situation, "Bosniaks who were part of reserve units who protested and left their units," they left their units simply by deserting in breach of the law without permission, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: When I said that they protested, this is just a summarised version of my statement. I did not say that they were protesting at home. They protested in Banja Luka, when there were hundreds of men there carrying arms. They felt safe and they protested -- the Yugoslav People's Army had already split into --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, may I stop you. May I stop you. Witness, I put it to you -- you are an intelligent man, as you've said. You know perfectly well that my question was not directed to the word "protested," and you're avoiding my question. My question is directed to the -- leaving their units. They left their units without permission in breach of the law, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: This form of desertion from the units is something that I am not aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you say -- it's your evidence here in your statement. Do you say they left their units with permission? They said to their commanding officer, I don't want to be here any more. Is it all right if I go? And their commanding officer said, Sure, off you go? It was desertion, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: I don't know what the commander told them, the commander who did not provide any food for them. At least that's what people told me. This was an army without the proper leadership. That was the time when the Yugoslav People's Army was being transformed into the Serbian army. I mentioned the mobilisation point in Banja Luka and the one in Han Pijesak. The Serb soldiers had their tents where is they had food, tinned food, beer, and everything that they needed, whereas there were other tents with Bosniaks in them; they did not receive any food. Nobody addressed them. Nobody talked to them. The officers ignored them. And I heard people talking about that, people who -- who returned and told us about that. There were also Bosniak officers, as well as the Serbian officers, and I suppose that they had agreed and that they said, There is not enough food for everybody. Let's leave people to go home but without weapons. That is something I am absolutely aware of. All the reservists who had left in that way, who had been mobilised either in Han Pijesak or in Banja Luka, they would return in this way. They would be sent home in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, let's not pursue this matter too much. It's not one of the core issues of the case. And I don't know whether there's that much disagreement between the parties on whether there was a legal basis for leaving. I mean, I'm not talking about whether there were reasons to do so but whether there was a legal basis to leave any unit. And we really enter into the realm of speculation where we say because of the lack of food and the uneven distribution of it, commanders might have said. I mean, it's really --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, may I say I 100 per cent agree, because not a single one of my questions was directed towards eliciting any of that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And frankly, I didn't want it. I didn't ask for it and I didn't want it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then is there any disagreement between the parties that there was no legal provision providing for someone who didn't want to go to Croatia to leave their units?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not in a position to put the Prosecution's position on that. What I am able to say is that in our submission the -- the facts that the witness have -- has referred to are facts that impinge upon the legality of their continued participation in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Departure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're doing the same as the witness does, and that is to rephrase my question only to answer a different question. I asked whether there was any legal provision which would allow someone to leave the unit, and I was not asking whether you might have good reasons to do so. And sometimes even if there's no legal provision, there are good reasons to do something. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, in direct response to your question, we would say that the matters that the witness has raised, I am sure that there would be a legal provision that would allow for those to be aired in any hearing for someone who has deserted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts is not entitled to express his opinion on that. There are different cultures here. But Mr. Margetts's opinion, he is sure that there would be a legal opinion. He shouldn't say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's move on to a different subject. Please move on, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: After all, they've got our system in Australia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- the second situation that I was referring to, Witness, is this -- and I just -- again, as His Honour has indicated, I don't want to ask you to explore the underlying reasons or justifications. I just want to make it clear. "Some units composed mostly of Bosniaks who were sent to Banja Luka were dismissed and sent back." You're talking there in summary about the situation where basically the commanding officers just came to the view that there was no value in maintaining these units because they were not getting cooperation and obedience and discipline and so they should disband these units because they were of no military value. That was -- that's the -- that's the position there, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: These were only just parts of the units with Bosniaks as a majority. In the army, there are officers in charge of security and those in charge of morale and guidance, and I am sure that there was an assessment that these units could not be used against the Croatian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You don't agree very simply, Witness, that there was clearly -- however it was done, there was clearly an assessment these units were no longer of sufficient military value to the -- to the army and they should be disbanded and the members sent home? Isn't -- isn't that -- the answer to that yes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: I've said that parts of these units with Bosniaks in them as majority, who were treated in a very bad way, for example, in Banja Luka, at the Assembly point where people were kept on just one tin of food over a period of several days.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But Witness --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, please, please do not answer a totally different question by giving your own justifications for what happened. I'm asking you about facts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you're asking for a -- just again, you've asked for the logics for sending them back. Mr. Stewart, the Chamber has heard a lot of evidence in respect of Muslims not very much inclined to participate in the war in Croatia. The Chamber has also heard of Muslims who arrived in Banja Luka and then were sent back. Whether that was logic or not, it does not need a lot of imagination with the attitude, as it appears from at least major parts of the evidence I was just referring to, that if I were a commander who had to go to Croatia, right or not, that I'd rather not rely entirely on those elements in my units. That goes without saying, whether the witness says it's logic, it's not logic. The witness in his statement did not speculate. We are now seeking justifications. We're seeking logic behind the matters. We'd rather stick to the facts. Yes, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was seeking no such thing, as I've made clear before.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But, Witness, this --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, here's the link.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, paragraph 15, you say "In October 1991 all equipment for territorial defence such as uniforms, helmets and so on were taken from Bosniaks. They would receive written orders to bring in their equipment and hand it over to the Territorial Defence authorities. Weapons had not been distributed to the majority of the Bosniak reserves, so they did not have to hand in -- have them to hand in. And then Bosniak reserves who had answered the mobilisation calls and had been dismissed had to hand in their weapons when they left their units and returned home." Now, the first question is: You say "they had received written orders to bring in their equipment and hand it over to the Territorial Defence authorities."
