Did you see any such written orders yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: Yes, I did see written orders, and I saw people with rucksacks on their backs who went to Sokolac, to the Territorial Defence building, to take their weapons and other equipment there. And on their way back, I saw them not carrying weapons. And that is how I learned that people did not actually have weapons. They only had equipment that they handed in. But this is all that happened after the attempt to use those units. And when they realised that yes, those units could not be used - and that's the logic of it that I'm talking about again - when they saw that these units could not be used, the men would be taken away, both the weapons and the equipment. This is now my logic, and I believe that that was the case actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, I just want to -- I don't want to spend long on this at all. I just want to get clear, then, how this relates to the categories you referred to a few minutes ago. You -- first of all, the Bosniaks who had answered the mobilisation calls and has been -- had been dismissed, as you describe it - for example, the ones that went to Banja Luka were dismissed and sent back - they had no weapons anyway because as they were dismissed, their weapons were taken away from them. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: The answer to your question concerning mobilisation, going to Banja Luka, a lot of things that happened there, their return, demobilisation in Han Pijesak, the return home, and several days later or several weeks later taking this equipment back, this is something I cannot answer with a simple yes or no. This was a process involving many events which led to the units being unusable in Croatia, disbanded and sent home. They were not allowed to take weapons home as the Serbs were, and they received a written order which I have seen with my own eyes. I saw people getting onto buses and taking their equipment back to the Territorial Defence in Sokolac and handing it back.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But this order, then, to -- or these orders to hand in weapons would apply, wouldn't they, to people who had deserted their units and taken their weapons with them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: Sir, Bosniaks, Muslims, have never been deserters. Throughout history, in the Turkish army, in the Austro-Hungarian army, in the Kingdom of Yugoslavia, in Tito's Yugoslavia, in the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, throughout history, not a single Bosniak has ever been a deserter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll put a different question to you, then, Witness. These orders applied to those Bosniaks who had protested and left their units, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: Entire units protested whether they were companies or parts of battalions. And 300 or 700 armed men protested because of the poor conditions and primarily --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Please answer my question, Witness. Do you need to know again what the question is? I'll give it to you anyway. These orders applied to those Bosniaks who had protested and left their units. Whatever the basis of the protest, it applied to those Bosniaks, didn't they, those orders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: Can you clarify what orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Witness. I'm going to give up. The -- the next question, Witness, is: These orders applied to Bosniaks who had refused to answer mobilisation call, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: I don't know such people, people who refused the call to mobilisation and broke the law. If you have any knowledge of this and any lists of such men from Sokolac municipality, you can show it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, you added the reference "the break the law" in your answer, Witness, but you're saying you don't know of any refusals by Bosniaks to answer the mobilisation call? Let's define it to Sokolac. Are you saying you don't know of any -- you never heard of any Bosniak in Sokolac refusing to answer the mobilisation call during the war in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: Men liable for military service, conscripts, or members of Territorial Defence units in a percentage in compliance with the law, there were people who were ill or abroad or who had other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, let me stop you. The question clearly is whether there were any Bosniaks who refused, not because they were ill, because they were abroad, but just did not want to respond to a mobilisation call. That's the question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the period I was referring to, I know of no such cases; that is, July/August 1991 until September. I am not aware that anyone refused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And after that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After that period, when they had handed back their equipment, they were not even called up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you have no knowledge whatsoever of Bosniaks refusing to answer a call for mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then it's time for a break, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a break of half an hour, which is a bit more than usual, due to the number of redactions. We'll adjourn until ten minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, the Chamber will first make a finding on your objection against the chronology. Anything --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- beyond the 1st of April because -- might be important for you to -- to know whether there's any cross-examination needed on that point. The Chamber does not as such reject evidence which consists of information provided by other sources to a witness on events in a municipality the witness had left already by the time of the events. The Chamber has accepted such evidence where it was introduced in a way which allowed the Chamber to establish whether a minimally required level of reliability existed to attribute any probative value to that portion of the evidence. In respect of the chronology - that's the list of events tendered by the Prosecution - in respect of that chronology, to the extent that it goes beyond the 1st of April, 1992, the Chamber finds that it is not in a position to establish a level of reliability due to the major lack of transparency of the sources and also in view of the limited talent the Chamber observes the witness has - just on his own, and not guided by proper questions - to clearly distinguish between facts and assumptions. And due for these reasons we find that we are not in a position to establish a level of reliability needed to attribute probative value to that part of the chronology. So therefore it's -- your objection is granted and there's no need to cross-examine the witness on those portions of the evidence. Yes, Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was a further addition to the material that was submitted, and that was a list of persons that were captured in Novoseoci, and in his statement he said, in fact, that those people were killed. I note that that event occurred, I think, in September 1992. So I'm assuming that that is encompassed within your ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Whatever events there are until the 1st of April, 1992 is -- all the rest taken prisoner and now -- it's -- you might not be surprised, Mr. Margetts, that the Chamber is quite hesitant to accept this kind of evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness may be brought in. Mr. Stewart, perhaps the course the cross-examination took until now is such that the Chamber would like you to finish the cross-examination today.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I -- I was going to say exactly this -- and perhaps it wouldn't be inappropriate for it to be transmitted to the witness. Your Honour, if the witness answers my questions, I am confident that I can finish by the end of the day. If he doesn't, then, Your Honour, it's simply unfair to expect me to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But then to continue and to see whether your questions will not be answered at future occasions is -- you might also keep in the back of your mind the ruling the Chamber just gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It was -- sorry, I beg your pardon, Your Honour, I didn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I didn't understand that as a ruling. Your Honour, with respect, it cannot be ruled that in advance of seeing whether the witness even observes minimal cooperation in answering the questions put that a time limit should be put. Your Honour, I'm saying I do expect to finish, but would Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- please then assist me strongly in assuring the witness does not continue to avoid answering the questions and reformulating them to his own taste.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I try do so. I'll continue to do so. Mr. Stewart, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, you described in paragraph 17 of your statement, this was, when you heard news about barricading. You were in Olovo at the time. You said that you -- you said: "The streets, cafes, coffee bars were full of Serbs," et cetera. "Many of these people were not from our area. I estimate that 20 per cent were from Rogatica, Pale, and Han Pijesak." What was the basis of your estimate as to where those people had come from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: This refers -- I estimated this on the basis of the number of participants in these protests and the blocking of the town, because the town of Sokolac has not more than 5.000 inhabitants, including women and children. That's the entire population. In my assessment and also the assessment of other people who were present or in some way involved in these events. This was between three and four thousand people who were there. So you can say that a large percentage of people had arrived from outside to support these protests.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And why specifically -- or how specifically did you assess that they were from Rogatica, Pale, and Han Pijesak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: A population of 5.000 inhabitants in Sokolac, they all knew each other. I'm referring to the adult men. You can remember several hundred telephone numbers. You can have a thousand friends. You can remember a certain number of faces. It's all a gift of God. So based on that and based on conversations with other people. And on the basis of people whom we didn't know who were there and who said they had come to our assistance, as they said, from Pale, Rogatica, Han Pijesak, and other places. So it wasn't hard to conclude that. This was a small town, not a large place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, come to whose assistance? You said, "They said they'd come to our assistance."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: That's what they said. Whenever they protested about something, they always said they were under threat. On the 10th of June, 1991 to block the town from all sides, all entrances, and organise a rally of some sort, for no reason. How else can we explain this?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You give evidence - it's paragraph 21 of your statement - that on the 20th of February, 1992 two brigades of paramilitaries that you described gathered, about 2.000 of them at -- it's Brezjak is the name given in your statement. Is that the same as we'd see on the map as Brezakovici or are those two different places?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: Brezjak is the real name.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's just north of the main town in Sokolac; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: I wouldn't say it was to the north. I would sooner say it was to the south-east.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, we can all look at the map in due course. The -- what's the source of your knowledge that two brigades were activated and about -- and 2.000 of them about gathered at Brezjak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: We, conditionally speaking, we Bosniaks, one of our fellow townspeople was employed in the Territorial Defence. He was a reserve officer of the JNA and he worked in the Secretariat for All People's Defence. And I think I told you from whom this Bosniak -- the Bosniaks in Sokolac learned that two brigades had been prepared for mobilisation. One was called the Light Romanija Mountain Brigade and the other was called the Mechanised Brigade and that the manpower was about 2.000. He didn't say with precision that it was 2.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Just moving on, then. In -- it's in paragraph 24 of your statement. You refer to what you describe as a new force Serb police of the SAO Romanija, and you say: "The chief of this police of this new force had the first name Cedo. I think his family name was Krajisnik." You're -- that's just a coincidence, is it? You're not aware of and not suggesting any family connection with Mr. Momcilo Krajisnik who's on trial here, are you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: It's a common last name, Krajisnik, not just among the Serbs. There are also quite a few Bosniaks bearing that last name. I don't think they were related in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then later on in your statement, paragraph 26, you talk about in the middle of -- at "the beginning of April 1992, a Bosniak, a factory watchman was killed in Podromanija." You say, "his name was Ahmet Cerimic and he was killed, you say, by Rade Abazovic," who was a member Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of the SDS. At that time he was one of the ones who manned a checkpoint close to the factory. If we take it he was a member of the SDS, you know of nothing, do you, to suggest that the SDS as an organisation was involved in or in any way brought about that killing, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: The SDS in waging its policy brought about a situation in which it was possible for one of its members to kill a man without being brought in or ever being punished. He has not been punished to date. It's up to Their Honours to evaluate what the responsibility of the SDS is for this. It's not up to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the question was whether you have any specific knowledge that the SDS instigated or sent him or anything of that kind, or that you just say he was an SDS member.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The SDS established a para-police. He was a member of it. And this made it possible for him to perpetrate this dishonourable act.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, the Chamber finds that there's no more specific evidence on this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- and then you say there were eyewitnesses to the murder. Are you able to name just one? Are you able to name any eyewitness?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Near that checkpoint was the house of a lady who worked in the psychiatric hospital. Her name was Havka Hrvat and she saw this incident. Unfortunately, her son Mirza was killed in her house a little while later before her very eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you refer to another murder, Ms. Hrvat. You say that he was murdered on the 15th of June, 1992 and that Zeljko Minic was responsible for that murder. You -- you know, do you, that -- yourself that Zeljko Minic was responsible for that murder?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: According to the statement made by his mother, Mirza's mother, the witness who knew the gentleman you mentioned personally, she claims that he committed the murder before her very eyes and her daughter was present also. She was 17 or 18. She was of age. So it's not just her but also Havka's daughter who were present when the son or -- and the brother were killed in the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just seek one clarification, Mr. Stewart, in this respect. Did you -- did they tell you or did you -- you were talking about a statement. Did you read a statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I was a refugee in Visoko, this lady, Havka, was a neighbour of mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So she told you; is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not just once. She told me that over and over again, and I always listened to her patiently because it was a way of relieving her sorrow for her only son who had been killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You -- you refer to an incident - this is paragraph 28 of your statement - on the 26th of March. You talk about "paramilitary units driving army trucks, looting, damage to shops." Partly destroyed by paramilitaries. And you say: "The police didn't take any action about this." Wouldn't the position have been this: That given the nature of what you describe, the police simply couldn't have taken any effective action?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: There were sufficient numbers of policemen, and they had sufficient weapons and equipment. I am referring to vehicles, communications equipment, and so on. They had sufficient access everywhere. So they could have stopped this unprecedented looting very efficiently. It was, however, the common purpose for parts of the municipality with a Bosnian majority to be deprived of food so that it would be easier to eliminate them when they were starving.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How many men do you say - we'll assume it was all men - how many men do you say were included in these paramilitary units who arrived driving army trucks on the 26th of March, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: There would usually be a jeep and a lorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, just give an estimate, please, of the total number of men.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: The territory was large, so on any one day the looting would take place in different places. Seven, eight, or ten paramilitaries were engaged in one place. I can give you those places or facilities. In Banja Lucica, in Kalinja --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Please just give an estimate. If you can't say, you can't say. And then please tell the Trial Chamber that. Otherwise, please give an estimate for the total number of men you say, if you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness, could you please answer that question, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: It appears that the answer has already been given in the previous answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it's not given. Mr. Stewart was asking about a total of the paramilitaries and the witness described a number of -- of a group of paramilitaries. So the witness at the same time said they went to several places. Could you give us an estimate of how many approximately, if you can, on these various places where they were, how many there were in total.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On that day, according to my estimate, including those who had given them orders, between 70 and 100 men were involved in the looting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In paragraph 30 of your statement, you say: "The military commander of SAO Romanija was Slobodan Batinic and Nedeljko Zugic was Minister for Information. All those appointments" -- or both those appointments, presumably -- "were done in secret." In what way were they done secret and kept secret from whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: When I was talking about secrecy, I was referring to the Bosniak population, they were not kept abreast of the situation. They could not learn through their representatives or in the Assembly or in any other way, they couldn't learn about those appointments. Only when rumours started circulating amongst the people or when on Radio Romanija somebody would appear and introduce themselves as the commander of the Territorial Defence or the minister of the so-called police, it was only then that we heard that, or maybe somebody said -- the anchor said, The Minister for Information will explain some events to you. And then it would be Nedeljko Zugic, the blacksmith, who would be that minister. I don't have anything against him. I know him personally. But how can you appoint a blacksmith as -- as a Minister for Information? This is -- this just is something that escapes me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, let's move on to the next question, Witness. You said -- at paragraph 33 of your statement that the Serb Crisis Staff "had been established during 1991" and it "held authority over the police, Territorial Defence all important functions." Now, Witness, there was no question of -- of that Serb Crisis Staff having that sort of authority during 1991, was there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: From the very establishment, he did have the authority and he had things under his control. Everything that was happening in a municipality - in this case, the municipality of Sokolac - it was the Crisis Staff and its decisions that prevailed and nothing else could be done. It was the Crisis Staff that usually comprised the president of the municipality, the president of the Executive Board or the local government, as it were, the Chief of Police, the commander of the Territorial Defence, and so on and so forth. So they had all the authorities in their hands. Whatever was being done, it was done under their control, according to their orders, and they were responsible only to the higher levels. And that's who they reported to, to the higher levels for everything that they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you say "he" -- you said, "He had things under his control" at the beginning of that answer. Were you talking about Mr. Milan Tupajic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: Milan Tupajic was the president of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you talking about Milan Tupajic when you said -- it's a very simple question, Witness. You talked about "him," "he," "his." Is that person you're talking about Milan Tupajic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: I can say that in Sokolac the president of the Crisis Staff was Milan Tupajic. And this is what I said. And if I mentioned the Crisis Staff and if -- if a reference is made to the president of the Crisis Staff in Sokolac, that was Milan Tupajic. He was the president of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Is it correct that a Crisis Staff at municipality level comprised not only SDS members but members of the SDP, which was under the leadership of Nijaz Durakovic? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: To talk about politics and to talk about Nijaz Durakovic and his members as members of the Crisis Staff, this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, I don't want you to talk about him in some general sense. I would like you to answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The first part of the question was whether there were any members of the Crisis Staff were SDP members.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am now concentrated. When there was a division of power between the SDS, the SDA, and other parties, all the key positions were taken by members of the SDS, the chief of police, the president of the court, the president of the Executive Board, the president of the Municipality. They were all SDS members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, I'll stop you. Were there any SDP members -- members of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to my knowledge, this was not the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Because I put it to you, Witness, that there simply was no Serb Crisis Staff that met at any time, or SDS Crisis Staff that met at any time before April 1992. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff of the Serbian people, I don't know whether it was known or not, existed even before that date. Many preparations were carried out even before the date that you have just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You've referred to people being killed in an attack on the village of Novoseoci. Would you agree that that was a Serb revenge attack following Muslim attacks on Serb civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: Sir, could you please tell me where the attack took place. That would enable me to answer you maybe.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, we start with the attack which -- about which you give evidence, which is, you say, "persons killed in an attack on the village of Novoseoci." And I think we can take it that you're talking about a Serb attack and that the persons killed were Muslims. That's -- that's correct so far, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: There was an attack by the Serbian army on a village with a Bosniak Muslim majority. 44 people were killed and 102 women and children were transported by buses to Sarajevo and expelled. This was on the 22nd of September, 1992. Amongst those 44 people who were killed, there was also one woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And it was a revenge attack in response to a number of Muslim attacks on Serb civilians, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the territory of Sokolac municipality, not only was not a single civilian killed, but no Serb had even lost a hair from their heads. Not a single house was torched. Not a single cow was taken away. Bosniak Muslim population of Sokolac municipality never ever committed anything illegal against the Serb neighbours. There's no evidence to the effect that any such thing had ever happened, and I'm sure that in the future no evidence will ever be revealed to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So if -- if I mentioned to you seven members of the Dautovic and Brdjanin families killed in the village of Tocionik that summer by Muslims, you know nothing of that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: Sir, and Your Honour, the Dautovic family was killed by the Serbs from Kalimanici village -- or rather, Tocionik village near Sokolovici. The eyewitness to the event is a person called Kerla. He is a Serb. And there's also Miroljub Krunic, who currently resides in Sarajevo. The latter took the first man into his car and transported him to Sarajevo together with his family to help them. So this is a humanitarian gesture that the latter person did. Based on this evidence and the testimony of some Serbs whom I wouldn't mention - there is a family Djeric, whom I know. There are allegations that the Djerics had killed this family. This man was a wonderful man. He had a very old mother. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: (redacted) They killed his son, his daughters, his old mother. They killed him and his wife. That is a terrible act that was committed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I'm looking at the clock. I'm also looking at the interpreters and technicians assisting us. How much time would you still need? The witness is now answering your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, I've noticed that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And we've been making tremendous progress. Your Honour, I only really have a couple more questions. If the witness does answer my questions, we shouldn't have a problem finishing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I ask the interpreters whether they're willing to assist us for a couple of more minutes and then -- you heard Mr. Stewart saying that it's only a couple of questions. For the technicians as well. Then we may proceed. Mr. Stewart, let's try to finish within the next seven to ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I shall certainly do my very best to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, you also nothing about -- I'm going to give you three or four names. I won't give you so many that you can't digest them. But Vukosav Belkovic [phoen], Jovan Veljovic, Rade Dragicevic, Ilija Macar [phoen] and his wife Slobodanka. Do you know anything about the killing of any of those people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: I don't know anything about those people. But as a human being, I would like to know something. If you have any information about that, I'd like to know as a human being if --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If the microphone could be switched off, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please tell me where those killings were committed, who committed them, if you know. If this is your deliberate interpretation of some events, I don't know what to say to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Witness, if you say you know nothing at all about any of these people, then I -- if you don't mind, I won't spend time giving you the information. The -- do you know the names of any of the Serb perpetrators of the attack on Novoseoci?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: Novoseoci? The attack on Novoseoci was carried out by the military police under the command of Momcilo Pajic, who is currently the head of land surveying department of the municipality of Kostolac. Between 400 and 450 soldiers were involved in the attack. The women who were expelled to Sarajevo identified 62 participants in the attack. When the crime happened and when the men were separated from the women and children and the women and children were loaded onto buses, Momcilo Pajic went to Sokolac and according to the testimony of these women, he came black in the face. They assume that somebody from Sokolac ordered Momcilo Pajic to kill all the men. It is only an assumption at the moment who it could have been; either Milan Tupajic as the head of the Crisis Staff, or general whose name I can't -- oh, it was Krstic, General Krstic, who was the commander at the time. This still remains to be seen. This is still in -- within the realm of speculation. I wouldn't go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, do you know anything about two of these Serb perpetrators of -- of that attack, the participants in that attack committing suicide subsequently?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: I've already said that the attack --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, do you know anything about two of the perpetrators of that attack committing suicide? If you don't, please say you don't.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: I know nothing of that. But if you will allow me, if the Court will allow me, I would like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, I don't know if the Court will allow you. I'm in the Court's hands. But I'm not going to encourage you, Witness, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you. I have one more question, a different topic, Witness. Well, I think it will be one. It might be just two connected.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- is it correct that you in either late 1990 or in 1991 informed Serb officials in your municipality that it was the intention of the Muslim community to set up their own parallel municipal organs in Kacina [phoen] and I think it's Knezina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: If I may give you just three sentences in introduction. The municipality of Sokolac has 11 local communes. Bosniaks are a majority in about five local communes. In one of these local communes, until the year 1957, there was a municipality that the communist powers, for reasons known only to them, had abolished. It was the desire of the population to have the municipality restored because of the local significance, local development, because the municipal territory was large. It was difficult to do, to perform different jobs. I may have mentioned in a conversation this desire; however, I say as I sit here -- I will still say that it would be good if there was a municipality there because of the people who reside there, irrespective of their ethnic background and -- and it is a good thing that the Bosniaks have returned. We live together. The mosque is being renovated, the one that was built in 1542. And I can say that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, witness, can we come forward from 1542, please, to just this: You did, in fact, take some -- or steps were taken by the Muslims to set such parallel organs in operation and they called themselves some such name as the Muslim militia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: At the beginning of our testimony, I said that Bosniaks, Muslims, did not have the opportunity to do any such thing. This may have been mentioned on one occasion in a private conversation with a colleague of mine, somebody from the SDS maybe even, that I said that it would be good for the Bosniaks to have Knezina as a municipality. Yes, I remember now that I did say once to the then-president of the SDS, and I told him, If you keep on insisting on your Autonomous Provinces --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Witness, you're answering my last question, which I thought you'd already answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question was, Witness 012, whether this wish that you once expressed in conversation ever materialised in establishing something which would be called the Muslim militia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Such an organisation did not exist in Sokolac municipality. And as far as I know, it didn't even exist in any part of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This is the first time today that I hear of such an organisation, of all the inconceivable things that were ever mentioned to me. This is really something that I hear for the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you answered the question. Mr. Stewart, any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Your Honour, one very brief question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: If I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Witness 012, when the SAO Romanija police were formed and the Serb police gathered at the Sokolac oval, how many police gathered at the Sokolac oval on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS KRAJ 012
utterances.text: I have described many events today, but I believe that this happened in March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a line-up --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were not asked when it happened. The question was how many police gathered at the Sokolac oval on that occasion, and that is when the SAO Romanija police were formed. Do you know how many either precisely or approximately were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Between 300 and 350, including the commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, we did intend to ask another question in relation to the payment system of SDK Sokolac, but I don't know that we have the time for that, and I just want to put that on the record in case it may result in us wanting to recall this witness at some stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Margetts, the Chamber has considered your request for one further question, but in view of the time, in view of the whole context we are in at this moment, the Chamber asks you to refrain from putting that question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then since -- since the Chamber has no questions for you, this concludes your testimony, Witness 012, taking that you, Mr. Stewart, have -- well, there could have been no questions triggered by the Bench, but also not by the one question put by the Prosecution. I'd like to thank you very much for having come to The Hague and to testify. We're happy that you're in a position that you can return home and that you don't have to stay over the weekend, which of course might not have been pleasant for you. We thank you very much for coming. We wish you a safe trip home again. Mr. Usher, could you please escort Witness 012 out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, as far as exhibits are concerned ...?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibits are Prosecution Exhibit P728 to P731A, all exhibits under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. They are admitted with the exception of -- now I don't see what the number is -- events on the territory of -- that's the chronology. Mr. Margetts, you are invited to provide a redacted version of that document so that any event after the 1st of April does not appear any more on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARGETTS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We will redact the exhibit P729.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So, then, 728 and 730 and following, as mentioned by Madam Registrar, are admitted. 729 is still pending until we have received the redacted version. I would like to thank the interpreters and the technicians very much for their patience. It's very often on Fridays that I am asking for this patience. Thank you very much. We will -- I'll not deliver the other decision we had in mind. I ask the legal officer to try to get the copies back so that they can be distributed to the next interpreter's team next Monday. We'll adjourn until next Monday, at 9.00, same courtroom. We adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 23rd day of May, 2005, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.08 p.m.,
